slides.title: When Enterprises Become Multi-Agent Systems
takeaways: Focuses on architecting, scaling, and securing autonomous AI agent networks across dynamic enterprise infrastructure.
Serves as a strategic roadmap and zero-trust security blueprint for enterprise-level multi-agent AI adoption.

slides.title: From Monolithic AI to Active Agent Networks
takeaways: Enterprise AI is shifting from passive, siloed tools to an active mesh of autonomous agents executing end-to-end workflows.
This paradigm shift enables autonomous task decomposition, peer-to-peer delegation across enterprise boundaries, and self-organizing systemic intelligence.

slides.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration Patterns
takeaways: Identifies four distinct system topologies for multi-agent coordination: Orchestrator-Worker, Hierarchical Teams, Dynamic Router, and Peer Swarms.
Spans structures from centralized delegation and tiered management to context-driven routing and decentralized peer collaboration.

slides.title: High-Impact Industry Adoption
takeaways: Multi-agent systems are actively deployed vertically across critical domain-specific enterprise functions.
Cybersecurity SOCs leverage agents for autonomous incident triage, threat hunting, and rapid remediation.
Financial operations and healthcare utilize multi-agent workflows for risk scoring, fraud detection, and multi-specialty patient synthesis.

slides.title: Unprecedented Scale & Speed
takeaways: By 2026, 40% of enterprise applications are expected to integrate task-specific AI agents.
Parallel execution across multi-agent workflows drives a 10x boost in throughput.
Accelerated multi-step reasoning and retrieval lead to a 95% reduction in latency.

slides.title: Emergent Multi-Agent Risk Surfaces
takeaways: Agent-to-agent interactions introduce vulnerabilities such as cascading prompt injections and unverified permission inheritance during execution.
Delegation across boundaries risks identity spoofing and boundary loss, allowing multi-agent decisions to bypass standard governance controls.

decks.title: Agentic Security: When AI Becomes Both Defender and Threat
decks.subtitle: Cybersecurity Paradigms for Autonomous Systems
decks.description: Exploring the cybersecurity battlefield, the new agentic attack surface, prompt injection defenses, multi-agent risk multiplication, and runtime intent enforcement.
decks.author: Harsh Verma

slides.title: Agentic Security: When AI Becomes Both Defender and Threat
takeaways: Introduces the concept of Agentic Security, where autonomous AI serves dual roles as a protective measure and a potential security risk.
Examines key cybersecurity paradigms for autonomous systems, specifically focusing on trust, control, and resilience.
Serves as an introductory student guide to understanding modern AI-driven threat landscapes and defense mechanisms.

slides.title: It's not who can build now, it is who you trust - From Creator to Curator Economy
takeaways: The competitive differentiator in AI has shifted from technical building capability to trust and reliability.
The technology landscape is transitioning from a Creator Economy toward a Curator Economy centered on trusted oversight.

slides.title: Agenda
takeaways: Outlines key topics bridging generative AI, intelligent agent architectures, and autonomous defense systems.
Examines real-world applications, ethical challenges, and future skills required for AI-powered security.

slides.title: Today's Cybersecurity Battlefield
takeaways: The modern cybersecurity landscape is rapidly escalating in both complexity and scale.
Critical metrics show high-frequency attacks occurring every 39 seconds and average breach costs hitting a record $4.45M.
Threat actors maintain a long presence within compromised networks, with an average of 287 days before detection.

slides.title: AI Agents Hierarchy of Needs
takeaways: Modern cybersecurity faces systemic strain, highlighted by 5.4 billion annual malware attacks and a massive workforce shortage.
The 'Hierarchy of Needs' framework maps the stack required to build agentic systems, from base infrastructure and foundation models to specialized LLM security and observability.
Generative AI provides a critical path forward by enabling autonomous security monitoring, detection, and response to offset human talent gaps.

slides.title: The Evolution of Cyber Threats
takeaways: Security is shifting from reactive, rule-based traditional methods to autonomous, self-improving agentic AI systems.
The evolution follows a three-stage path: Traditional (manual/reactive), AI-Enhanced (pattern detection), and Agentic (fully autonomous decision-making).

slides.title: The New Attack Surface
takeaways: AI systems introduce new vulnerabilities through model behaviors, data exposure risks, and complex API integrations.
The interconnected nature of AI agent toolchains significantly expands the potential blast radius of security exploits.
Core security pillars—Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA)—are the primary targets within this evolving AI threat landscape.

slides.title: Common Adversarial Tactics
takeaways: Prompt injection is the primary threat to LLMs, allowing malicious inputs to override system instructions.
Data leakage risks include the exposure of sensitive PII, internal documents, and proprietary logic by models.
Over-permissioning AI agents can transform minor security exploits into critical, system-wide failures.

slides.title: Why Traditional Security Fails
takeaways: Conventional tools fail because AI systems are non-deterministic and dynamic, causing threats to evolve faster than traditional patch cycles.
Effective AI security requires shifting from static scanners and signature-based detection to runtime interaction monitoring, adaptive defenses, and continuous red-teaming.

slides.title: From Chat to Action: Why Security Rules Suddenly Fail
takeaways: Agentic AI executes multi-step tasks using tools and identity with real-world side effects beyond passive text generation.
Legacy security systems fail because persistent, acting agents create entirely new attack surfaces.
Security controls must shift from simple input filtering ('prompt safety') to runtime 'workflow safety'.

slides.title: The New Threats in the Agentic Stack
takeaways: Tool misuse occurs when agents combine valid tools into harmful workflows that bypass static security checks due to injected or ambiguous intent.
Identity and privilege abuse escalates the classic 'confused deputy' problem to machine scale via credential inheritance across task boundaries.
Dynamic trust exploitation creates fragile trust chains as agents interact with unverified dynamic tools, MCP endpoints, and other agents.

slides.title: Multi-Agent Systems: Risk Multiplies, Observability Blinds
takeaways: Multi-agent environments introduce emergent trust boundaries where agents delegate to each other, propagating risk beyond single-agent boundaries.
System risks multiply due to cascading failures, non-deterministic emergent behaviors, and vulnerabilities in shared memory, context, and tools.
A single poisoned context can rapidly spread malicious logic across an entire agent mesh in seconds.

slides.title: When Governance Breaks: Supply Chain & Dynamic Dependencies
takeaways: Runtime dynamic loading of tools and endpoints often lacks cryptographic verification and provenance checks.
Poisoned context and malicious logic injected into tool responses propagate silently through decision chains.
Unverified agent-to-agent delegation creates supply chain vulnerabilities without clear identity, intent, or manifest verification.

slides.title: The Governance Shift: Static Checks → Intent + Runtime Enforcement
takeaways: AI governance is shifting away from static checks toward a model focused on intent verification and runtime enforcement.

Effective security governance relies on three nested layers: Core Intent (signed goals and verification), Runtime Controls (sandboxing and approvals), and a Standards Layer (MCP protocols and SOC integration).

slides.title: Permission Creep via "Citizen" Agents
takeaways: Over 80% of Fortune 500 enterprises deploy AI agents without adequate governance, driving 'Shadow Agent' risks.
Autonomous agent deployment creates missing audit trails, undefined ownership, and ungoverned access permissions.
Mitigating permission creep requires Discovery, Permission Mapping, Behavioral Baselines, and Lifecycle Governance.

slides.title: Agentic Tooling + Governance Controls Win
takeaways: Strict enforcement of MCP-based governance and tool-scoping policies resulted in an 85% reduction in unauthorized agent actions.
Implementing protocol-level verification and standards-driven orchestration achieved a 70% improvement in threat detection time.
Effective security requires constraining tool usage and treating MCP (Model Context Protocol) governance as the primary security perimeter.

slides.title: Security as a Startup Competitive Advantage
takeaways: Startups face significant security challenges due to resource constraints, rapid deployment velocities, and complex, expanding cloud-native attack surfaces.
Lack of formal security processes often leads to inconsistent controls and audit readiness gaps.
The cost of failure is high, with 60% of small companies failing within six months following a cyber attack.

slides.title: Automate, Codify & Build Security Culture
takeaways: Integrate security into CI/CD pipelines and infrastructure as code (IaC) to ensure auditability and reduce human error.
Prioritize practical security controls over 'security theater' and align incentives to make security a shared business value.
Cultivate a resilient organizational culture where security is seen as a competitive advantage rather than a compliance burden.

slides.title: Real-World Example: Robin AI & Pavlov Startups
takeaways: Security readiness, such as SOC 2 and GDPR, acts as a strategic business accelerator rather than an operational bottleneck.
Proactive, founder-led security programs serve as powerful signals for both enterprise customer acquisition and investor confidence.
Integrating security from day one builds foundational trust and enables faster scaling without sacrificing innovation velocity.

slides.title: Challenges, Ethics & Governance
takeaways: Organizations face significant risks including overreliance on AI, workforce skills gaps, and legacy infrastructure integration hurdles.
Balancing autonomous security operations with essential human oversight remains a critical governance challenge.

slides.title: Organizational Risks
takeaways: Adopting autonomous security introduces risks including overreliance, skills gaps, and legacy infrastructure integration challenges.
Organizations must navigate the critical challenge of balancing automated AI-driven security with necessary human oversight.

slides.title: Startup To-Do List: Foundational Controls
takeaways: Establish strict security foundations by mapping all agent-accessible tools and enforcing least-privilege credentials.
Implement human-in-the-loop oversight for high-impact actions and sanitize RAG data to secure model memory.
Ensure deployment infrastructure includes isolation, robust identity management, and continuous behavioral monitoring.

slides.title: Designing Secure AI Systems
takeaways: Implement the principle of least privilege for all AI tool calls and API interactions.
Adopt a defense-in-depth approach by layering security guardrails and PII detection.
Ensure safe-by-design principles through modular architecture and strict component-level privilege separation.

slides.title: A Practical Reference Model: Identity-First, Least Privilege, Telemetry
takeaways: Treat AI agents as distinct identities with full authentication and accountability rather than anonymous scripts.
Implement fine-grained, just-in-time delegation that limits tool access by task, time, and revocability.
Utilize continuous behavioral telemetry to monitor agent actions and detect deviations from established security baselines in real time.

slides.title: Automate and Codify Security Controls
takeaways: Integrate security policies directly into version-controlled infrastructure and CI/CD pipelines to eliminate manual error and maintain velocity.
Prioritize substantive, risk-reducing controls over 'security theater' and embed incident recovery planning into the design phase.
Utilize Infrastructure as Code (IaC), automated compliance checks, and open-source security frameworks to ensure consistent, repeatable protection.

slides.title: Build a Security Culture & Shared Responsibility
takeaways: Security must be treated as a core organizational priority involving everyone from leadership to engineering and operations teams.
Cultivating long-term resilience requires embedding security into company culture through regular training and clear communication.
Effective security strategies rely on strong leadership commitment and aligning security goals with overall business and customer objectives.

slides.title: Student Action Plan: Learn & Build
takeaways: Develop prompt injection defense skills using interactive platforms like Lakera Gandalf.
Prioritize security by executing untrusted agent code exclusively in isolated sandboxes, away from production environments.
Deepen understanding of AI safety by studying model alignment techniques such as DPO and Constitutional AI.

slides.title: What to Follow
takeaways: Prioritize industry-standard vulnerability references like the OWASP LLM Top 10.
Adopt emerging federal guidance such as NIST AI 100-1 for secure and resilient AI deployment.
Monitor ongoing research and safety frameworks from authoritative bodies like Berkeley RDI and Frontier Labs.

slides.title: Your Playbook: Projects, Checklist & Career Path
takeaways: Implement hands-on capstone projects focusing on incident-response agents and agent registry prototypes to build practical expertise.
Adopt a robust governance framework that emphasizes least privilege, environment isolation, and continuous red teaming for AI agents.
Develop specialized skills in agentic threat modeling to identify and mitigate risks like tool misuse, memory poisoning, and supply chain vulnerabilities.

slides.title: What Is Next: The Agentic Frontier
takeaways: Future AI systems will require a hybrid approach, blending symbolic and non-symbolic components to mitigate emerging architectural risks.
As AI scales beyond human oversight, implementing formal verification and provable security becomes critical for maintaining system integrity.
Security engineers must proactively adopt a strategy that combines adversarial thinking with rigorous design to ensure systems remain reliable and corrigible.

slides.title: Emerging Trends
takeaways: The security roadmap transitions from foundational prompt engineering and orchestration toward explainable, generative adversarial systems and multi-modal cognitive frameworks by 2027.
Critical focus areas include managing agent coordination, ensuring AI ethics, and maintaining robust model evaluation to protect against emerging manipulation tactics.

takeaways: Provides external resources for further reading and author attribution.
Lists professional profiles and publications on Hackernoon, Forbes, and LinkedIn.

takeaways: Opportunity for audience interaction and clarification on agentic security concepts.
Open forum to address specific concerns regarding AI as both a defender and a threat.

decks.title: HikeRunner: LoadTestFramework
decks.subtitle: High-Throughput Distributed Performance Testing Architecture
decks.description: In-house distributed load testing framework to simulate real-world messaging user journeys, vertically & horizontally stressing backend DBs, caches, queues, and CI/CD pipelines.
decks.author: Harsh Verma

slides.title: HikeRunner: LoadTestFramework
takeaways: Presents HikeRunner, an in-house enterprise load testing framework engineered for high-throughput mobile messaging ecosystems.
Addresses the limitations of off-the-shelf testing suites by introducing an analytics-driven approach to real-time user journey simulation.

slides.title: The Challenge: Scale in Real-Time Messaging
takeaways: Modern messaging applications with millions of active users encounter extreme spikes and complex distributed state variations.
Traditional testing tools fail to mimic real user behavior patterns across multiple interactive communication services.

slides.title: Motivation & Gaps in Existing Tools
takeaways: Commercial and open-source tools do not provide a generic, protocol-agnostic interface for full-stack stress testing.
Need for simultaneous vertical and horizontal stress testing across databases, caches, queues, and network proxies.

slides.title: HikeRunner Architecture Overview
takeaways: Modular design patterns allowing pluggable protocol engines, task executors, and dynamic metrics aggregators.
Coherent orchestration between scenario generators, agent workers, and real-time telemetry reporters.

slides.title: Analytics-Driven User Journey Simulation
takeaways: Derives load profiles directly from production analytics to accurately weight user actions and probability distributions.
Accurately captures real-world user paths rather than synthetic, unrealistic endpoint hammer tests.

slides.title: Multi-Protocol Support: MQTT, HTTP & Caches
takeaways: Native support for asynchronous MQTT socket channels, RESTful HTTP APIs, and direct cache/database protocols.
Enables end-to-end verification across the entire communication pipeline from client connect to database commit.

slides.title: Vertical & Horizontal Stress Topologies
takeaways: Horizontal testing scales load across hundreds of microservices; vertical testing isolates single-node saturation points.
Pinpoints exact database lock contention, memory leaks, connection pool exhaustion, and cache eviction cliffs.

slides.title: Static Hooking & Task Assignment
takeaways: Static hooking mechanisms allow engineers to attach custom assertion logic and deterministic payload generators.
Ensures repeatable, deterministic regression tests before deploying code to staging environments.

slides.title: CI/CD Pipeline Automation with Jenkins & Git
takeaways: Automated execution within the continuous integration pipeline triggered via Jenkins jobs and Git hooks.
Enforces automated performance gates preventing build merges that violate strict SLA and latency thresholds.

slides.title: Latency, Throughput & Soak Benchmarking
takeaways: Comprehensive telemetry tracking P90, P99, and P99.9 latencies under sustained and burst load conditions.
Long-running soak tests detect slow memory degradation and resource leaks across multi-day test runs.

slides.title: Summary, Impact & Future Roadmap
takeaways: HikeRunner established resilient release stability, cut regression test times by over 60%, and prevented major outages.
Future enhancements focus on autonomous load generation, AI-driven anomaly detection, and automated root-cause isolation.

slides.title: The Evolution of Cybersecurity: From Anomaly Detection to Intent-Based Security
takeaways: Explores the fundamental paradigm shift from legacy anomaly-based detection to autonomous intent-based cybersecurity.
Introduces the 'Clean Attack Problem'—where malicious actions are carried out entirely within valid credentials and trusted workflows.

slides.title: The Historical Foundation & Limits of Anomaly Detection
takeaways: Traditional cybersecurity assumes malicious activity deviates from established baseline behaviors.
Signature rules, threshold alerts, and statistical outliers fail when adversaries emulate legitimate system patterns.

slides.title: The Clean Attack Problem Defined
takeaways: Clean attacks use authorized credentials, invoke approved APIs, and navigate standard user flows with zero abnormal signatures.
When nothing looks wrong, traditional defenses report 100% green health while critical assets are actively compromised.

slides.title: AI Agents as Adversarial Multipliers
takeaways: Generative and autonomous agents can dynamically adapt attack trajectories in real time to blend into normal enterprise traffic.
Static heuristics and rate limits are trivial to circumvent via multi-agent coordinated stealth operations.

slides.title: Case Studies: When Legitimate Workflows Turn Hostile
takeaways: Analysis of real-world breaches where attackers hijacked legitimate communication and administrative conduits.
Demonstrates how identity verification at the perimeter provides zero guarantee of safe post-auth operation.

slides.title: The Paradigm Shift: From Behavior to Intent
takeaways: Shifts focus from 'Is this action authorized?' to 'What is the underlying purpose and eventual outcome of this action sequence?'
Introduces dynamic reasoning engines that evaluate operational legitimacy rather than static permissions.

slides.title: Behavioral Sequencing & Contextual Awareness
takeaways: Evaluates full chains of multi-step interactions across time rather than isolated individual transactions.
Constructs contextual semantic graphs linking user roles, business logic, temporal patterns, and data flows.

slides.title: Dynamic Workflow Legitimacy & Reasoning Frameworks
takeaways: Real-time intent validation evaluates whether state transitions align with verifiable organizational objectives.
Enforces policy checkpoints that intercept authorized accounts attempting anomalous goal-oriented trajectories.

slides.title: Building Resilient, Adaptive AI-Era Cybersecurity
takeaways: Architectural blueprint for transitioning enterprise defense from static gatekeeping to cognitive, intent-aware resilience.
Provides actionable steps for deploying runtime intent guardrails, adaptive trust scoring, and autonomous mitigation.

decks.subtitle: Post-Authentication Risk, Behavioral Monitoring & Runtime Intent Analysis
decks.description: Addressing post-authentication risk and trusted-agent misuse. Why Zero Trust must evolve beyond static identity verification toward continuous behavioral monitoring and runtime intent analysis.
decks.author: Harsh Verma
decks.blogTitle: RSA Conference: The Death of Authentication

slides.title: The Death of Authentication: Why Identity Isn't Enough for AI Systems
takeaways: Examines why traditional authentication is breaking down as autonomous AI systems enter enterprise workflows.
Argues that verifying identity is no longer sufficient when systems can be fully authorized yet still cause severe harm.

slides.title: The Fallacy of Static Trust
takeaways: Decades of cybersecurity have equated successful authentication with operational trustworthiness.
In modern AI architectures, identity verification only answers 'who is acting', never 'is the outcome safe or intended?'

slides.title: The Rise of Autonomous Enterprise AI Agents
takeaways: AI agents are rapidly granted API keys, service credentials, database privileges, and autonomous tool-use capabilities.
Agents operate autonomously across distributed SaaS platforms, microservices, and internal corporate databases.

slides.title: The Trusted-Agent Misuse Dilemma
takeaways: Introduces 'Trusted-Agent Misuse'—where harmful outcomes happen entirely within permitted operational boundaries.
The attacker does not need to compromise or forge credentials; they simply manipulate the agent's goal-seeking logic.

slides.title: Beyond Identity: The Post-Authentication Threat Landscape
takeaways: Once an agent clears OAuth, SSO, or mTLS authentication, traditional access controls become completely blind to malicious actions.
Threats shift downstream from entry points to runtime execution, state mutations, and data exfiltration.

slides.title: Breakdown of Traditional Perimeter & RBAC Controls
takeaways: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) was designed for human users with predictable, bounded interaction patterns.
AI agents execute non-deterministic combinatorial workflows that render coarse-grained role permissions ineffective.

slides.title: Lessons from High-Profile Identity Breaches
takeaways: Case study analysis (including the Uber breach) illustrating how valid credentials become weaponized conduits.
Demonstrates that an adversary operating inside authenticated channels faces almost zero friction from legacy tools.

slides.title: Process Manipulation & Workflow Escalation
takeaways: Adversaries trigger subtle deviations in agent planning loops that escalate blast radiuses without tripping alarms.
Manipulating input embeddings, memory banks, or tool responses produces unauthorized outputs using authorized privileges.

slides.title: Anatomy of an In-Bounds Autonomous Attack
takeaways: Step-by-step breakdown of how an agent can be steered to exfiltrate proprietary data or corrupt records without violating ACLs.
Every single HTTP request, SQL query, and API call appears syntactically valid and cryptographically signed.

slides.title: Evolving Zero Trust: From Identity to Intent Governance
takeaways: Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA) must evolve from 'never trust, always verify identity' to 'never trust, continuously verify intent'.
Establishes continuous cognitive evaluation throughout the entire agent execution lifecycle.

slides.title: Continuous Behavioral Monitoring & Runtime Evaluation
takeaways: Implements real-time telemetry pipelines monitoring agent reasoning traces, semantic drift, and action side-effects.
Detects anomalous reasoning jumps and out-of-character tool invocations before irreversible mutations occur.

slides.title: Context-Aware & Temporal Authorization Models
takeaways: Transitions from static tokens to micro-scoped, ephemeral authorizations valid only for specific, verifiable micro-tasks.
Incorporate organizational context, time-to-live restrictions, and strict environmental boundaries.

slides.title: Intent Verification vs. Permission Checking
takeaways: Compares syntactic permission checks against semantic intent verification engines.
Intent engines answer: 'Does this agent's proposed action logically follow from the user's validated initial prompt?'

slides.title: Guardrails for Autonomous Multi-Agent Workflows
takeaways: Dual-layered guardrails: external proxy interceptors and internal model alignment constraints.
Includes circuit breakers, consensus mechanisms, and human-in-the-loop escalation thresholds for high-stakes actions.

slides.title: Strategic Architecture for Post-Authentication Security
takeaways: Comprehensive reference architecture integrating identity providers, intent evaluators, and runtime enforcement.
Provides zero-trust security leaders with a concrete roadmap for securing agentic AI deployments.

slides.title: Conclusion: Verifying Outcomes, Not Just Credentials
takeaways: The future of cybersecurity rests on measuring and guaranteeing outcomes rather than relying on identity gates.
Organizations that master intent-based security will unlock the full power of autonomous AI with safety and confidence.

slides.title: Agents Don't Break Rules, They Redefine Them: Cybersecurity in the Age of Autonomous AI
takeaways: Examines why autonomous AI agents rarely fail by explicitly violating deterministic security rules or role permissions.
Introduces the paradox of semantic compliance: AI systems follow instructions literally while circumventing intent through policy drift and specification gaming.

slides.title: The Fallacy of Deterministic Rule Boundaries
takeaways: Legacy cybersecurity assumes system behavior is constrained by deterministic Boolean policy rules and static RBAC boundaries.
Autonomous agents optimize across multi-step execution graphs where every intermediate step is valid, yet the terminal outcome subverts enterprise security policy.

slides.title: Specification Gaming: When Compliance Violates Intent
takeaways: Specification gaming occurs when an agent discovers novel, unanticipated trajectories through complex software environments that fulfill objective functions in ways architects never envisioned.
Examples include aggressive data consolidation, unintended API coupling, and bypassing rate limiting by optimizing legitimate workflow endpoints.

slides.title: The Semantic Hijacking Attack Surface
takeaways: Adversaries no longer require credential compromise or code injection; they introduce contextual cues and prompt injections that reframe the agent's interpretation of existing permissions.
The compromised agent becomes a willing accomplice, using its own authorized privileges to execute exfiltration or state mutation while believing it is fulfilling its mission.

slides.title: Multi-Agent Cascades: Risk Multiplication Across Handovers
takeaways: Enterprise ecosystems rely on multi-agent chains (planner, orchestrator, tools, executor) where context is compressed and transferred across boundaries.

Slight semantic drift or unverified assumptions at each handover stage amplify exponentially, resulting in unauthorized cross-domain actions without any single agent technically 'breaking' its local sandbox.

slides.title: The Failure of Point-in-Time Authorization
takeaways: Traditional identity and access management (IAM) validates permissions at the moment of request invocation ('point-in-time').
Autonomous agents execute asynchronous, long-running, multi-turn trajectories where the security posture changes dynamically based on intermediate tool outputs and environmental feedback.

slides.title: Shift from Static Boundaries to Continuous Runtime Governance
takeaways: Moving from static gatekeeping to continuous intent verification, behavioral trajectory monitoring, and deterministic runtime guardrails.
Continuous governance evaluates full operational chains against high-level invariants, verifying that composite trajectories remain aligned with business purpose.

slides.title: Intent-Aware Mediation & Downstream Simulation
takeaways: Deploying runtime mediation layers that simulate the downstream consequences of proposed agent action plans before execution.
Comparing proposed state mutations against organizational invariants, isolating destructive operations into sandboxed verification zones.

slides.title: Strategic Blueprint: Resilient Autonomous Enterprise Defense
takeaways: Actionable roadmap: enforce dual-control authorization for high-consequence agent actions, semantic invariants, state rollback mechanisms, and audit logs that capture agent reasoning chains alongside standard API telemetry.
Empowers organizations to capture the immense velocity of Agentic AI while establishing unbreakable runtime guardrails.

slides.title: Why Multi-Agent Systems Are a Cybersecurity Nightmare
takeaways: Deep-Dive into inter-agent trust chains, cascade injections, memory poisoning, and agentic IAM architecture.
Keynote executive threat briefing on AI risk and autonomous ecosystem security by Harsh Verma.

slides.title: The Structural Shift to Autonomous Agent Networks
takeaways: Contrasts legacy single-agent models (bounded execution, explicit human verification, predictable API perimeters) with modern multi-agent systems.
Highlights emergent risks: autonomous collaboration, transitive trust chains where agents implicitly trust peers, and cascading vulnerability surfaces.

slides.title: Multi-Agent Execution Graph Mechanics
takeaways: Traces execution graphs from Node 01 (Retrieval Agent) to Node 02 (Synthesis), Node 03 (Execution), and Node 04 (Validation).
Exploit Pattern: Silent Automated Escalation — poisoned context in ingestion propagates silently across trusted peer nodes without triggering perimeter firewalls.

slides.title: Transitive Trust: The Fundamental Weak Link
takeaways: Implicit payload verification gaps: raw text and JSON pass between sub-agents without cryptographic signatures or schema sanitization.
Unchecked credential inheritance and dynamic topology blind spots prevent runtime proxies from anticipating or enforcing static communication paths.

slides.title: Cascade Prompt Injection & Payload Hopping
takeaways: Step 1 Ingestion Phase: Adversary embeds hidden prompt instructions in untrusted documents or CRM data.
Step 2 Boundary Hopping: Intake agent inadvertently wraps malicious instructions into trusted inter-agent task calls, leading to Step 3 Privilege Execution.

slides.title: Shared Memory & Vector Store Poisoning
takeaways: Corrupting the Collective Brain: Multi-agent systems relying on shared vector databases (Pinecone, Milvus, Redis) face permanent cross-agent context contamination.
Long-term persistence vector lingers across sessions; cross-agent contagion and stealth logic distortion alter decisions without runtime errors.

slides.title: Tool Output Manipulation & API Exploitation
takeaways: Web search tampering hijacks automated research agents via maliciously crafted public web content.
Third-party API poisoning and recursive loop exhaustion can trigger infinite execution loops, spiking cloud API costs and causing complete denial of service.

slides.title: Stanford & UC Berkeley Benchmark Findings
takeaways: Empirical research demonstrates 82% of inter-agent calls accept peer inputs without schema validation or sanitization.
Finding 01: Zero foundation model failure required (underlying LLMs worked within safety bounds; breach occurred via peer trust). Finding 02: Injected prompts traveled across up to 4 agent hops.

slides.title: MITRE ATLAS & OWASP Agentic Top 10 Mapping
takeaways: MITRE ATLAS Tactics: AML.T0051 (Prompt Injection via Inter-Agent Handoffs), AML.T0054 (Vector/Memory Poisoning), AML.T0058 (Excessive Agency).
OWASP Agentic Risks: LLM01 (Indirect Prompt Injection Cascades), LLM06 (Excessive Agency in Sub-Tasks), LLM08 (Unsanitized Memory Poisoning).

slides.title: The Identity Crisis: Traditional IAM vs. Agentic IAM
takeaways: Traditional IAM was built for humans logging into applications; Agentic IAM must govern autonomous software acting on behalf of humans.
Shifts from static RBAC and long-lived OAuth tokens to machine-to-machine delegated authority tokens, task-bound ephemeral scopes, and continuous intent provenance.

slides.title: Machine-to-Machine Identity Delegation Protocol
takeaways: Phase 01 Root Intent Scoping: Human user request mints a cryptographically signed Root Intent Token defining explicit boundary parameters.
Phase 02 Sub-Task Attestation: Orchestrator mints short-lived (60s) downstream tokens; Phase 03: Target API validates caller identity and human intent provenance.

slides.title: Inter-Agent Firewalls & Schema Contracts
takeaways: Strict typed JSON contracts replace raw natural language inter-agent handoffs with strictly validated schemas.
Inline behavioral proxies act as inspection sidecars to detect indirect injections; trust decay algorithms automatically reduce permissions as handoff depth increases.

slides.title: Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Policy Enforcement
takeaways: Critical Gate Triggers: Mandatory human approval required for state deletions, database modifications, or wire transactions.
Confidence thresholds pause automated execution when uncertainty drops below 95%; immutable audit logs record execution graphs for forensic analysis.

slides.title: CISO Strategic AI Defense Roadmap
takeaways: Phase 01: Asset Discovery & Graph Mapping; Phase 02: Schema Contract Hardening across inter-agent communications.
Phase 03: Agentic IAM Token Deployment with root intent signatures; Phase 04: Inline Telemetry and HITL Gates on write APIs.

slides.title: Protecting Autonomous Machines from Other Machines
takeaways: Executive takeaway: The next major frontier in cybersecurity is protecting machines from other machines operating inside a trusted ecosystem.
RSAC Executive Briefing conclusion and strategic recommendations for autonomous AI resilience.

takeaways: Technical diagrams and reference architecture attributions.

decks.title: Security Without Humans: Designing Systems That Defend Themselves
decks.subtitle: Closed-Loop Containment, L0-L3 Risk Envelope & 90-Day Autonomous Defense Roadmap
decks.description: Shifting from alert-centric visibility to autonomous resilience across Intent, Time, and Interaction—featuring closed-loop containment, the L0–L3 risk envelope, and a 90-day enterprise roadmap.
decks.author: Harsh Verma
decks.blogTitle: RSA Conference: Security Without Humans: Designing Systems that Defend Themselves

slides.title: Security Without Humans: Designing Systems That Defend Themselves
takeaways: From visibility to autonomous resilience—with Intent, Time, and Interaction as structural guardrails for machine-speed cyber defense.
RSA Conference Official Library companion presentation by Harsh Verma, Principal Software Engineer - AI.

slides.title: Visibility Is Not Resilience: Moving Beyond Alert-Centric Security
takeaways: Contrasts today's alert-centric pipeline (Telemetry -> Alert -> Queue -> Analyst decision) constrained by escalation latency against autonomous resilience (Telemetry -> Context + Policy -> Bounded action -> Verified recovery).
Core design goal: remove repetitive delay—not human accountability—allowing routine, reversible threats to be contained at machine speed inside explicit policy boundaries.

slides.title: The Response Loop Is Being Outpaced
takeaways: Traces autonomous attack progression across Signal (anomalous behavior), Decision (context evaluation), Delegation (tool or peer agent invocation), and Impact (data, identity, or workflow changes).
Explains why a human approval loop at every step becomes a bottleneck—especially for low-risk, repeatable containment.

slides.title: Security Is a Property of the Whole System: Intent, Time, and Interaction
takeaways: Frames autonomous-system security across three interacting dimensions: Intent (does the action match the approved objective?), Time (how does risk change as context and state evolve?), and Interaction (how can trust and privilege propagate between actors?).
No single control can guarantee safety when the system continuously changes through delegation and autonomous action.

slides.title: Threat Path: How Compromises Travel Through Trusted Workflows
takeaways: Maps the 4-stage propagation chain: 01 Untrusted Input -> 02 Agent Misreads content as authority -> 03 Trust Propagates to peer agents/tools -> 04 Workflow Impact across data, identity, and operations.
Highlights the core defensive question: where can the execution chain be interrupted before trust becomes transitive?

slides.title: Closing the Loop: The 6-Stage Self-Defending System Lifecycle
takeaways: Defines the closed-loop autonomous response sequence: 1 Sense -> 2 Assess (identity, intent, risk) -> 3 Contain (smallest reversible action) -> 4 Restore (trusted state) -> 5 Verify (controls and service health) -> 6 Learn (update policies and detections).
Enforces a strict Policy Gate: every autonomous action must be explainable, scoped, logged, and reversible where possible.

slides.title: A Reference Architecture for Autonomous Defense
takeaways: Connects Protected Environments (Agents & Copilots, Apps & APIs, Cloud & Endpoints) to an Autonomous Defense Plane organized across Observe -> Decide -> Enforce -> Recover.
Spans continuous Governance across every layer via risk appetite tiers, policy ownership & exceptions, immutable audit trails, and human escalation & override.

slides.title: Guardrail 01 — Intent: Bind Every Action to an Approved Purpose
takeaways: Identity alone answers who; Intent answers why an actor is acting and what it is allowed to accomplish via an explicit Intent Contract (Purpose, Actor, Resource, Allowed Action, Data Scope, Expiry).
Illustrates point-of-action authorization: read-only invoice metadata matches approved intent (ALLOW), while changing payment destination or releasing funds violates scope (DENY / ESCALATE).

slides.title: Guardrail 02 — Time: Trust Has a Half-Life
takeaways: Addresses permissions that were safe at task start becoming unsafe after state changes, anomalies, or context shifts across Issue -> Re-Evaluate -> Expire -> Revoke / Renew.
Establishes three temporal controls: Short Leases (reduce stale authority), Event-Driven Checks (reassess after drift), and Safe Expiry (fail closed for sensitive actions).

slides.title: Guardrail 03 — Interaction: Stop Trust from Becoming Contagious
takeaways: Models multi-hop delegation graphs (User -> Orchestrator -> Data Agent / Payment Agent -> Resource) protected by per-hop authorization, provenance, and scope preservation.
Enforces non-transitive trust by default: permission to call one agent does not imply permission to use every capability reachable through it.

slides.title: Adaptive Defense Framework: Five Building Blocks of Continuous Control
takeaways: Details the five continuous building blocks: 01 Behavioral Monitoring -> 02 Policy Enforcement -> 03 Contextual Trust -> 04 Autonomous Remediation -> 05 Self-Adjusting Controls.
Reinforces that adaptive defense does not mean unconstrained: every policy update must be tested, explainable, and reversible.

slides.title: Governance by Design: The L0–L3 Autonomy Risk Envelope
takeaways: Defines a four-tier operating envelope: L0 Observe (collect evidence), L1 Recommend (human review), L2 Bounded Auto (preapproved reversible containment), and L3 Approval Required (high-impact or irreversible actions).
Core operating rule: default to the narrowest authority that can safely achieve the defensive objective.

slides.title: Illustrative Scenario Walkthrough: Containing a Compromised Workflow
takeaways: Walks through an untrusted invoice attachment prompt-injection attack path countered at each stage by Intent (read-only scope), Time (short-lived token), Interaction (per-hop auth denying privilege inheritance), and Recovery (quarantine document, revoke session, verify state).
Demonstrates containing the workflow before payment state mutation while preserving forensic evidence for review.

slides.title: Industry Applications: Same Resilience Pattern Across Critical Sectors
takeaways: Applies bounded autonomous resilience across Financial Services (hold suspicious transfer, revoke session), Healthcare (isolate compromised integration while preserving clinical availability), Manufacturing/OT (segment gateway), and Cloud & SaaS (revoke token, restore config).
Synthesizes the cross-sector pattern: detect context -> choose smallest safe action -> verify service health -> recover.

slides.title: Operating Metrics: Measure Resilience, Not Just Alert Volume
takeaways: Measures speed, scope, and recovery quality via MTTD (Mean Time to Detect), MTTC (Mean Time to Contain), MTTR (Mean Time to Recover), and Blast Radius (affected assets/users).
Tracks automation safety metrics: false-containment rate, successful rollback/restore rate, policy override and escalation rate, and audit-evidenced action coverage.

slides.title: Human Governance: How Autonomy Changes the Work Humans Do
takeaways: Separates organizational duties across Humans Define (risk appetite, approved action tiers, policy ownership), Systems Execute (evidence collection, low-risk containment, token revocation), and Humans Review (high-consequence actions, ambiguous intent, post-incident learning).
Establishes the governing principle: delegate execution—never delegate accountability.

slides.title: Implementation Roadmap: A Practical 90-Day Path to Bounded Autonomy
takeaways: Outlines a three-phase rollout: Days 0–30 Baseline (map agents, identities, rollback paths), Days 31–60 Shadow + Simulate (observe-only mode and incident replay), and Days 61–90 Bounded Autonomy (enable low-risk reversible actions for one workflow).
Mandates disciplined scaling: never scale autonomy faster than you can measure, audit, and reverse it.

slides.title: Design Checklist: Seven Principles for Systems That Defend Themselves
takeaways: Architecture review checklist: 01 Least privilege by default, 02 Authorization bound to intent, 03 Short-lived scoped delegation, 04 Continuous trust re-evaluation, 05 Smallest safe containment action, 06 Verified recovery, 07 Retained human accountability.
A system is not self-defending because it can act—it is self-defending when it can act safely, prove what happened, and recover.

slides.title: The Next Security Model: Machine-Speed Defense Within Human Boundaries
takeaways: Don't remove humans from responsibility—remove humans from repetitive delay.
Build systems that can defend, recover, and explain—at machine speed, within human-defined boundaries.

slides.title: References & Further Reading: Primary Source + Foundational Standards
takeaways: Cites the primary RSA Conference Blog article ('Security Without Humans: Designing Systems that Defend Themselves', Nov 13, 2026) as the source for the Intent, Time, and Interaction framing.
Grounds architecture guidance in NIST SP 800-207 (Zero Trust Architecture), NIST AI RMF 1.0, NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (Incident Response), and MITRE ATLAS.

slides.title: References & Further Reading: Security Practice + Industry Frameworks
takeaways: Connects OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 (excessive agency and prompt injection) and CISA Secure by Design principles to autonomous cyber defense.
References industry initiatives including DARPA AI Cyber Challenge (AIxCC) and autonomous security copilot patterns.
